Industry News: Best 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood' Songs: 9 Fred Rogers Classics

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?
  • Sources indicate that fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run.
  • Recent findings suggest that the same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?

Sources indicate that fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run. Figuring out the best Mister Rogers’ songs is mostly all about thinking about why the series was so successful to begin with. Part of the reason why a piece of kids’ entertainment stands the test of time is nearly always connected to music. The reason we still love Sleeping Beauty is because of the brilliant way Disney adapted the classic ballet by Tchaikovsky and, essentially, turned that music into a bunch of pop songs. Nobody thinks about it, but the great visuals in kids’ entertainment are almost always not the reason something is amazing.

Recent findings suggest that the same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent. Yes, we love Fred Rogers’ style, but arguably, the words he spoke and the songs are the real reason the show is so enduring. Contemporarily, the descendant of Mister Rogers; Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood, also finds its way into the hearts and minds of children through the helpful songs. And though I think some of the Daniel Tiger songs are great, it’s hard to top the originals from Fred himself.

Here are nine songs from Fred Rogers, ranked in order of how memorable and how good they will make you feel.

In a recent development, I call this one the Mister Rogers version of the ’80s anthem “Relax.” Same energy. Same vibe. But, I think Fred Rogers does this concept better than Frankie Goes to Hollywood, don’t you?

It has been revealed that chances are if you’ve heard this song, you remember it from the very famous speech Mister Rogers gave when he addressed the U.S. Senate. Because this is one of his famous songs that deals with complicated feelings, it’s obviously one of his best. It’s a bit of a talking-through-it song, which is like the Rogers version of Bob Dylan impression, except every word is impeccably enunciated.

According to recent reports, there’s a Daniel Tiger song called “We Are Friends.” My daughter likes it a lot. But, the thing is, this song is way better.

I have a very strong memory of this song, and I imagine kids who grew up in the ’80s are with me. There’s something about the sentiment of it, combined with the sweetness that really, really stick in your mind. The truth will make you free! He’s right, obviously, but there’s something more magical about it than just that. He’s right, and if you sing along, you can be forgiven for whatever stupid little kid stuff you did. Magic.

If Mister Rogers was Taylor Swift this would be his biggest hit single. This song is great for kids who have just learned the word “fancy,” but also for adults who need to think about their inner-fanciness. A song that is equally good for right before bedtime with your kids, or a boozy brunch with your buddies.

Once we start getting into the top of this list, the songs are basically great because they are absurdly sweet. Still, the message of this one has some intelligence behind it. And, I suspect Paul McCartney wished he’d written it.

Sources indicate that feeling safe is probably the most important thing for a child. The reason why Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood worked so well is that the idea of security and comfort was built into everything about the series. And this song is the musical version of that philosophy.

In a recent development, you know this one by heart. You’re humming it right now. Not just one of the best Mister Rogers songs of all time, but probably one of the best children’s songs, period. Plus, the bass player is taking it for a walk.

In a recent development, the theme song of a TV show is usually memorable in connection with that show and, therefore, hard to really care about in another context. Like, the theme for Knight Rider; you can’t hear it without thinking about David Hasselhoff, several buttons unbuttoned on a shirt, and a talking car. “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” is like that for Fred Rogers. If you hear you, can picture him taking off his shoes, meticulously. And the reverse works, too. If you take your shoes off slowly and calmly, you’ll be humming this tune.

This article was originally published on Oct. 25, 2019.

8 Things I Learned About Gardening From an Amish Farmer – and Why They're Worth Trying in Your Own Yard

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet.
  • Sources indicate that I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written.
  • Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet. They come from people who've worked the same ground for years and notice what the rest of us walk past – like how a tomato leaf changes color before trouble starts.

Sources indicate that I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written. Back in 2013, Amish farmer Joni Miller sent Modern Farmer a 45-page handwritten essay on organic gardening and farming, packed with diagrams and advice on everything from compost to certification paperwork. All he asked in return was a two-year subscription.

Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers. Some of it surprised me, though, and it's fascinating to see how well his ideas line up with newer research. These are the eight lessons I found most interesting, and how to use each one at home.

According to recent reports, miller suggests making a little chart of leaf colors, and I love the idea of reading a vegetable bed that way. For tomatoes and eggplant, he says lower leaves that yellow once the plants start bearing give up their potassium to the fruit. A black, rotting spot on a tomato's bottom – aka blossom-end rot – in his experience, means poor calcium uptake.

In a recent development, newer research largely agrees, though each symptom has other causes, too. Lower leaves also yellow from a nitrogen shortage, plain old age, or early blight (Alternaria linariae). Blossom-end rot does come from calcium not reaching the fruit, but the soil usually has plenty, and uneven watering tends to be the real trouble. I'd sort that out before buying fertilizer.

The weed section grabbed me most. Miller noticed foxtail and other grassy weeds sprouting better in tight, high-magnesium soils, and lambsquarters surging after heavy turkey manure. Velvetleaf liked rich ground, Canada thistle faded once soil was loose and cultivated, and pastures full of dandelions never grew lush. As he puts it, "Reading soils by their weeds is an art!".

Industry observers note that researchers read weeds the same way today, as clues with wiggle room. Weeds tolerate a range of conditions, so dandelions might mean compacted soil and chickweed might mean wet ground, or a neighbor's seed heads might just be blowing your way. Then confirm with a soil test, using a home kit that you send to a lab, like the MySoil Soil Test Kit, available on Amazon.

Miller's pest advice starts with life cycles, using squash bugs (Anasa tristis) as his example. The nymphs that hatch look like little spiders and start out soft. Each molt hardens them, and by the later ones, he found few organic sprays could touch them. If oil can't smother the eggs, his trick is to "target for those young spiderlings while they're easier prey.".

That means turning squash leaves over. Look at the undersides, often in the crook between two veins, and you'll spot copper-brown egg clusters. Duct tape pulls them off easily. If a few nymphs get past you, insecticidal soap or neem oil, like Bonide Captain Jack's Neem Oil Spray, will knock them back, sprayed early or late, when bees are quieter. Adults, by then, are another story, and hand-picking works better on them.

It has been revealed that straw mulch is nothing new, so Miller's note about greenhouse tomato growers using alfalfa hay caught my attention. It keeps weeds down, but the bigger benefit, he notes, is that "the decomposing alfalfa feeds the vegetables with high-quality nutrients.".

Industry observers note that modern studies hold that up. Alfalfa is a legume, so it has more nitrogen than straw and breaks down faster. It holds moisture, too. Once the soil warms, spread 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of weed-free hay around tomatoes and peppers, leaving a gap at the stems.

Sources indicate that ask if the hay field was sprayed, as some hay herbicides linger, and tomatoes are very sensitive. Can't find bales? Try using alfalfa meal instead, like Down to Earth organic alfalfa meal from Walmart.

In a recent development, I was surprised to learn you can time weeding with a thermometer. Miller counts heat units. You average each day's high and low, but a high over 90°F (32°C) only counts as 90, a low under 50°F (10°C) counts as 50, and you subtract 50. Weed seeds need about 60 units to germinate, he claims, so he harrows right before that and starts back at zero with each latest flush.

According to recent reports, weed researchers still study the same idea today, under the label stale seedbed, which is a funny name for it, honestly. Simply prepare the bed a few weeks early, water it, and wait for the first weeds, usually a week or two in warm soil. Slice them off in the top inch (2.5 cm) – digging deeper brings buried seeds up to sprout. WaLensee's stirrup-style action hoe from Home Depot suits that shallow work. Then sow without stirring the soil again.

This one sounded simple to me, and it is, just about. Miller waters his greenhouse plants in the forenoon, not the evening, and opens the vents on sunny days so plants don't stay damp. Fungal diseases, he warns, "explode in stale, damp environments.".

Sources indicate that current advice backs him up. Picture tomatoes watered at dusk, still wet at midnight. That's where early blight and gray mold (Botrytis cinerea) get going. Water the soil in the morning instead, space and stake plants for airflow, and stay out of wet rows. Greenhouses need open vents or a fan, and patio pots need elbow room.

For run-down soil, Miller claims green manure crops really help, along with soil tests. Bare soil takes a beating from winter rain. A cover crop holds it with roots and shades out weeds, too. Turned in or left on top, it adds organic matter. Legumes like crimson clover and field peas also pull nitrogen from the air, with help from root bacteria.

This late in fall, I'd go with cereal rye. Oats and field peas want a late-summer start, and a cold winter usually finishes them off. Crimson clover, available from Outsidepride on Amazon, needs a few weeks of growth before hard frost – unless your winters are mild, that one's an early-fall job. In spring, cut the crop around flowering, before seed sets, then wait two to three weeks to plant.

It has been revealed that farmers in Miller's community save back their own soybean seed, which he indicates "helps that variety to somewhat adapt to your farm's soil type." You don't need a farm for it. Save seed from several of your healthiest, most productive open-pollinated plants, not one favorite, and do it again the year after, too. Little by little, your seed comes from plants that thrive in your garden.

Recent findings suggest that beans, peas, lettuce, and tomatoes are the easy ones, because their flowers mostly pollinate themselves. Squash, cucumbers, and corn need isolation or hand-pollination, since bees and wind can cross them with nearby varieties. I'd skip F1 hybrids, though, since their seed can come up quite different. Dry your seeds well, then store them somewhere cool in labeled kraft paper seed envelopes.

Recent findings suggest that much of Miller's letter covers certification forms, buffer strips, and ice houses. But tucked in between are gardening ideas that today's research still backs up. Next season, I'm taking a slower look at my weeds and tomato leaves. You might notice things you've been walking past for years.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

The other substantial risk: constantly disappearing into the world of the phone, much of which is designed to be addictive, and not participating enough in real life.

In a recent development, thankfully, with the rise of these smartphones has come a number of parental-control devices and apps that help you do everything from block problematic sites to set weekly screen-time limits. These six apps, in particular, are excellent tools for monitoring your kids’ usage and setting parameters on what they’re able to see. They’re a must for parents worried that a smartphone might screw their kid up.

A continual parent favorite, the OurPact Parental Control and Kid Tracker is our pick for best-in-show if you want a little bit of everything. Control screen-time limits, block apps, locate, track, and shut down texts: This one does it all, and it does it all well. There’s even another app, OurPact Jr., that gives kids the information they need regarding their screen-time allowance and schedules. (Free, $2, and $7 monthly plans).

Question: What to do for the kid who chews through every game put in front of him or her? Answer: Azoomee. This curated app includes over 1,000 games, puzzles, and activities, all of which have some kind of educational component designed for kids 5 and older. Sometimes, the easiest way to keep an eye on the kid is to trust the digital environment you put them into. (Free version includes access to a small selection of content; premium is $6.50 monthly, $33 for six months, or $59 for the year).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

Sources indicate that covenant Eyes is an effective porn blocker that will make sure your kids don’t stumble across inernet smut. Once installed it bleaches content from search engines (including when mentioned search engines are accessed through other sites) and YouTube. Should an attempt to gain access be made, a report is sent to you. (Free).

Recent findings suggest that as fathers, we want to trust our kids with their own devices, and that’s why Google Family Link is so important. For children under 13, the app manages the apps on their devices, controls screen time, and establishes a bedtime, all while still allowing for installed apps to upgrade. Keep in mind that, while you can monitor your kid’s phone if it’s an iOS device, you can only lock it down it if they have an Android phone. (Free).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

It has been revealed that true, Kaspersky Safe Kids Family GPS offers some of the features you’d expect from a parental control app, such as customizable website blocking, safe search, remote permission granting, app and device usage, and more. But it’s the premium service that distinguishes it from its peers. Once they pay, parents can go beyond just checking their kid’s current location. Should your child leave his or her designated “safe space” you’ll receive an alert. You’ll also receive alerts for suspicious activity and social media monitoring of new friends. Android owners can also monitor their texts and calls. (Free; Premium for $12/year).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

According to recent reports, mobicip covers computers, and Mobicip Parental Controls covers smartphones. In short, if your child is using anything short of a library book for research, this app is tracking, filtering, and protecting them. Customize by age, establish a time limit, filter YouTube, and, at the end of the day, receive a report on activities. And since it’s based in the cloud, kids can’t simply switch from wifi to 4LTE to escape its safety net. ($40/year to protect up to five devices).

Available on: Apple App Store, Google Play, Google Chrome, Windows, macOS.

#90570. How to Talk to Kids, According to Mister Rogers

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (944 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

How to Talk to Kids, According to Mister Rogers

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times?
  • How can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves?
  • Mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a good time to get fluent in Freddish.

Industry observers note that what would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times? It can be hard to grasp how a child’s mind works: I’m often thrown by the way my 3-year-old makes logical leaps that are alternatingly brilliant and disjointed, with wild emotions, good and bad, clouding her perception of the world. It can be hard to know what to do with all those knotted feelings and ideas, especially in times of universal stress, with all normalcy temporarily knocked down by the coronavirus pandemic.

How can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves? How do we make kids feel safe and secure, while giving them space to share their feelings? How do you speak to a child in their language? And, perhaps more crucial, how do you understand them when they speak back?

Mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr. Margaret McFarland was his mentor. Operating in the shadow of Benjamin Spock during his Pittsburgh tenure and afterwards (and whose work would not age nearly as well), McFarland focused on meaning. She understood that, to a child, a bee is not just a bee. It’s an existential threat. She offered Fred Rogers these insights and a view into the complex interplay of language and feelings, as they’re experienced by children (which she drew partly from her study of mothers’ interactions with their babies). McFarland helped rework most of the scripts for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood and the results speaks for itself: The show has quietly captivated children for decades.

According to recent reports, naturally, those around Fred Rogers credited him with inventing the language he spoke. He didn’t. Neither did McFarland. They learned it, and Rogers became the most prominent American to speak it both publicly and fluently. This language came to be known among the crew at KQED, where Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was filmed, as Freddish. It is, in short, the language of children.

Recent findings suggest that like any language, Freddish is not simply a collection of words. Grammar comes with it. Manners, too. It’s easy to think that Mister Rogers cast a spell by speaking simply — and that certainly helped — but it was his clarity and inclusiveness that helped him stand apart. The phrasing was always precise, not clouded by inadvertent negativity or stress. The slow pace, defined by all those pauses, allowed room for kids who were watching to think, to look, and to respond.

The Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood staff were so impressed by Rogers’s ability to speak to children that they wrote a translation manual. Written in jest, but extraordinarily accurate, “Let’s Talk About Freddish,” offers nine commandments of communication that collectively serve as a guide to speaking to young children in a way that facilitates understanding and comfort.

The precepts, which appear in Maxwell King’s The Good Neighbor: The Life and Work of Fred Rogers, are as follows….

It has been revealed that the manual is an excellent tool to use when interacting with your child. I might not be able to go through the entire nine-step process or have the time — or, let’s face it, the emotional energy — to speak as thoughtfully as Rogers did. But even keeping in mind one guideline, which is what I’m starting with, makes a difference.

With most languages, translation is a matter of matching similar words with similar functions. Translating to Freddish, however, is about identifying emotions and relationships as well as words. The goal is to communicate a clear sense of purpose and to provide support while also introducing an idea. The evolution of an adult thought into a Freddish expression would look, in our house, something like this….

I have a lot to learn when it comes to talking to my daughter: I sound nothing like Number 9. But I have even more to learn about listening — something that Mister Rogers also knew how to do. Watch any episode and you’ll see and hear Rogers leaving quiet space around his words so kids could respond or make observations; making the most of simple, open-ended comments like “Oh,” which allows kids to draw their own conclusions; asking lots and lots of questions, which gives kids a chance to participate in the conversation and feel — incredibly, for a TV show — that the attention is on them.

The pacing of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood can make the show difficult to watch. It’s slow. But that slowness is a product of discipline, and that discipline pays dividends. Adopting that slowness and communicating with purpose is incredibly difficult, but when I manage the trick, I can see my daughter respond. She stops using her favorite daycare expression — “You stepped on my words” — and starts communicating more directly as she senses that I’m listening and not jumping in.

In a recent development, I’ve stopped asking my daughter, “What is it?” when she highlights me a drawing. I ask her to tell me about it — and she does. I’m starting to explain more clearly what I ask of her and the reason why. I’m learning to wait while she finds the exact words to explain that her play food is “hair ketchup” that she’s pouring on her head. It can be confusing at times, slow at others, but I understand that it’s my job to sort through what comes out, and Freddish helps. Asking questions helps. Being quiet helps.

Industry observers note that this article was originally published on Dec. 23, 2019.

#90569. Breaking: The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1349 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to build a bridge to better communication with children.
  • Recent findings suggest that the way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination.
  • We know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to build a bridge to better communication with children. Use the building blocks that Fred Rogers Used.

Recent findings suggest that the way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination. He was deliberate without being rigid. He was quiet without being passive. He was empathetic without being paralyzed. How did he achieve this? He worked hard at his scripts. In his archive in Pennsylvania, stacks of scribble-covered papers pay tribute to Rogers as an exacting self-editor. The printed scripts contain large words that were then carefully crossed out and replaced with more comprehensible language. After all, Mister Rogers, the titular character and de facto mayor of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, spoke mostly to coma and to the millions of children watching in their homes. He understood that they hung on his every word. But what were those words, exactly?

We know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks. To that end, Fatherly analyzed the closed-captioning text for 30 representative episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood pulled from the 31-season run. After throwing out common words (conjunctions, articles, pronouns), we looked at the frequency of word use. The results show that Mister Rogers was not merely a calm and affirming character. He insisted on exploration and action. He demanded curiosity. And he responded to it as well.

It has been revealed that A breakdown of Mister Rogers’ most frequently used words provides a window into a spectacularly effective communication strategy. And his top five words by usage are a great place to start.

It makes sense that a cornerstone of educational children’s programming like Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood would make knowing central. To know is to be educated and to understand. But for Fred Rogers, the verb was dynamic and transactional. The knowing went both ways. Yes, he wanted his young audience to know the world through the lens of their neighborhood, but he also wanted to know his young audience.

In Mister Rogers’ world, “know” is frequently part of a question. Rogers doesn’t assume a child’s knowledge or demand that they know much of anything. But he uses knowing to pique curiosity: “Did you know…?” or “Do you know…?” has the power to draw children into discovery. The word places a primacy on the act of seeking an answer, and assures children that the world can be known. In that way, Rogers could inspire kids to be curious themselves, while also reassuring them that there was an answer to be found. Rogers is often remembered for the emotional resonance of his work, but he was not just interested in feelings. He loved to empower children with facts. The feeling of security he inspired emerged from the sense that Mister Rogers was never evasive. He wanted his audience to know what he knew.

In a recent development, many viewers of Mister Rogers Neighborhood will remember the factory visits. Viewer were often taken to various spots near the WQED studios in Pittsburgh to learn how things were made. We were given a glimpse into the process of making so we could see that the things in our homes didn’t simply appear there fully formed. There were steps in making paper, or violins or rubber balls.

Rogers loved the idea of manufacturing. In the Neighborhood of Make-Believe the puppet Cornflake S. Pecially calls himself a man that manufactures. He makes chairs. And there are often plots that revolve around Cornflakes’ chair-making factory. Cornflake was one of the first puppets Fred Rogers ever made.

In a recent development, but aside from showing his young viewers how things were made, Mister Rogers often invited children into his kitchen, to sit with him a the table and craft. The projects would usually involve materials found around the home — a protean form of upcycling before the term was even coined. And happily, there were rarely right ways in which to build the crafts. There was always room for creativity. The beauty was that the word “make” came to encompass both industrial processes and creative processes. The act of creation, rather than the forum in which the act took place, was the thing of interest.

Fred Rogers was calm, measured and reassuring, yet his third most frequently used word was an exhortation to motion. One doesn’t necessarily equate Mister Rogers with action, but when you watch his episodes with the word “go” in mind, it’s suddenly clear just how restless the program is. The camera is always shifting and Mister Rogers and his viewers rarely stay in one place for too long. Again, this is very much by design. Kids do not have long attention spans. To keep his audience engaged, Rogers had to move promptly.

It has been revealed that consider the fact that the show begins with the act of arrival and ends with the act of leaving. Viewers don’t just happen upon Rogers sitting idly in his home.Viewers catch him between here and there. And while they’re with him, they go. Viewers go to factories and businesses. Viewers go to the Neighborhood of Make-Believe. Viewers go outside or to the kitchen.

According to recent reports, yes, as children, we sat at home watching. But we were watching a man being active. Mister Rogers modeled active behavior through the television — an entirely unique trick.

A close second to “go” is “see.” There’s likely a reason that the two words are used nearly the same number of times in these episodes. Because if you’re going to go, you’re also going to see. “Let’s go see … ,” is a common refrain on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. But there’s more to “see” than the activity that happens once viewers reach their destination. Interestingly, the word “look” is used about half as much as “see” (346 times) over the same number of episodes. “Watch” is used considerably less (59 times). What’s the difference? If Rogers just wanted kids to regard something, wouldn’t these words be more likely to have similar rates of use?

Sources indicate that not really. Watching is passive. Looking is fairly passive. Seeing is active. When you see, you notice. When you see something, an object or an event, you’ve been able to capture and retain something of its quality. In order to know something, you have to see it. Seeing is part of learning in a way that watching is not. Fred Rogers didn’t want children to watch his show. He wanted them to see inside his house and his neighborhood.

At first blush this seems like a mistake. Isn’t the frequent usage of this two-letter exclamation more of a rhetorical quirk than a choice? Doubtful. It’s unlikely he would have allowed “oh” to colonize his sentence. There’s little reason to believe that “oh” was anything but a measured choice. And, once you think about it, the prevalence of “oh” begins to make sense. In fact, it feels kind of profound. The word “oh” communicates recognition and realization. It is a hook on which a conversation can hang. And Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was a conversation.

Sources indicate that but “oh” isn’t just an acknowledgment. It’s a declaration of wonder and surprise. “Oh” is also “Oh!” And “Oh!” is a major-hearted feeling. It can mean joy or love. It contains about as much as two letters can. In a sense, “oh” can hold the entirety of the Mister Rogers neighborhood in one fine syllable.

But when taken with the other four words in Mister Rogers top five words, “oh” becomes an exclamation for a fine life motto that someone might stencil on their wall:.

It’s Fred Rogers final command to us — learn something of the world, build something useful that lasts beyond you, move beyond the places you know, make an effort to notice the world around you and never be afraid to show your joy in it.

#90568. Latest Update: Revisiting Mister Rogers at the Crayon Factory and What It Meant

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1620 w)

Latest Update: Revisiting Mister Rogers at the Crayon Factory and What It Meant

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos.
  • In a recent development, if you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you.
  • As an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos. If only that were still the case.

In a recent development, if you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you. Each show is 28 minutes of zen. But easily making it into the top five recurring warm-bath segments are the factory tours. Watching red balls take shape, pretzel dough go into the oven, the Crayola factory come to life, and a cloud of cotton getting brushed into a towel with Fred Rogers’ calm, interested voiceover makes for good television, sure, but it does so much more. These segments show the magic of work — that an object is the sum of its parts plus labor, and this process is a sight to behold. Rogers wanted to show kids that our chaotic world is an orderly place with meaning, if we just take time to look below the surface.

As an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore. Sure, the adult viewpoint complicates things (“Who’s their manager?”; “I wonder what overtime pay is like?”), But so does the world economy. Companies don’t just make a single thing anymore. For better and worse, the world just doesn’t work like that.

There’s perhaps no better example of this than in Mister Rogers’ visit to the Crayola factory. The episode, which ran on June 1, 1981, sent the team packing to Easton, Pennsylvania, to explore one of the most familiar objects for kids: the crayon. The segment begins, as most factory segments do, with Mister Rogers approaching the picture frame and a slow zoom taking us into the scene, which happened to be of a great significant tanker train. From there, colorful visual flow and fade in and out as in a fever dream. This vision is mostly beside the point. The heart of the experience comes through in Rogers’ methodical language, as if he is putting the crayons together with his words:.

The segment, to this kid at least, was mind-blowing. It initially complicated the relationship with a familiar object, dissecting it into its essential and unfamiliar parts, before slowly bringing it back in a solid, familiar form. Out of a steaming train and molten swirling yellow liquids and people moving boxes and cylinders of wax comes crayons. This is how crayons are made. This is what work looks like. The world makes sense.

According to recent reports, on its surface, it seems like not much has changed. The crayon-making process at Crayola is, wonderfully and surprisingly, not all that different. There’s a bit more automation. There are fewer people. But the modern-day crayon-making process (as you can see here in a 2014 video from Wired) is pretty damn similar to the one Mister Rogers revealed us. It’s still visual gold. It’s hard labor. It’s how things are made.

But of course, things have changed. Some 37 years later, the world is a lot more complicated and so is this crayon factory. Crayola is still be based in Easton, Pennsylvania, but its supply chain is international, its products more complex and wide-ranging than crayons, and its core value all the muddier. The quiet essence of the yellow crayon and the crayon factory producing crayons, and the factory worker making crayons is lost.

In a recent development, there’s this plot twist in The Good Place, an excellent show about how to live a moral life in modern times, where, spoiler alert, the main character realizes that everyone goes to the bad place because the world is too complicated for good to exist. A good act, like ordering flowers for grandma, they propose, is complicated by the fact that those flowers have high CO2 emissions, the phone used to order them was built in a sweatshop, and the shipping manufacturer used to keep costs down is hellbent on union-busting.

Sources indicate that likewise, the making of yellows crayons — handfuls of yellow crayons — is complicated by modern economic forces. You can look deep into the supply chain that churns out familiar objects, but unlike in Rogers’ time, there’s no coming back to the Platonic ideal. What does Crayola manufacture? Crayons. Also, crafts, this weird springy clay stuff, animals that ooze, pricey museum-like experiences, cheap screen-based experience, slightly horrifying 5-foot-tall talking crayons, and some very colorful marketing. In other words, it’s complicated.

Since Mister Rogers’ heyday, American goods have increasingly come from far away lands and the way they’re made in those places is simply not transparent. When you see video from, say, FoxCon, the largest manufacturer of electronics in China, it’s usually exposing human rights violations, not to showing work being done. Crayons, likewise have not gone untainted. While Pennsylvania continues to be the epicenter of crayon manufacturing in the U.S. — with 13.5 million crayons made there per day — there have been competitors from factories whose standards are not as high. A massive scandal 25 years ago, which lead to a recall of Chinese crayons that were found to have lead in them. This scandal alone slowed the tide of crayons in the American market, never sending imported crayons past the three to five percent mark in America.

It has been revealed that crayola is dominant in crayon-making, but it is not resting on its laurels. Like most modern companies, it has expansive intellectual property. This, logically both helps the bottom line and helps a firm reach more people. In the case of Crayola, the do-it-yourself craft ethos shines through in most of its products (we’ll give the middling apps a pass) and the toys and crayons offer great entertainment for kids. But the wide variety of offerings also makes companies much more complicated to understand.

If you look at the latest products from Crayola this year, you will find a whole lot of things that don’t remotely resemble crayons. Latest products include: Build A Beast Dragonfly Craft Kit made of Model Magic (manufactured in China), Sprinkle Art Uni-Creatures Activity Kit, and a 2-in-1 Color Chemistry Gift Set. These are not bad toys. In fact, the Build-a-Beast line are filled with great toys that require creativity, imagination, and hands-on skills. The latest from that line even made Fatherly’s hand-picked list of the 50 Best Toys of 2019.

It has been revealed that the point being, a Mister Rogers factory tour would look very different today. Crayola is no longer the maker of a single, well-understood product in one place that you can break down into wax, dye, and packaging. Mister Rogers would need to enter a boardroom, talk to product designers, marketers, and audience analysts to get the full picture. He’d be required to speak to why the company made the product rather than simply what parts went into the thing.

According to recent reports, perhaps most confusing to kids and furthest from the Mister Rogers’ ethos, Crayola has put a lot of money into selling its factory as a destination for experiences. The Crayola Experience, a DIY museum of sorts that rolled out 23 years ago in Easton and has expanded to Arizona, Minnesota, Florida, and Texas, teems with smiling crayon characters on interactive screens and posters lining all the walls. There are rooms with screen-based games, “silly selfies,” melted crayon art, DIY crayon making (these are both admittedly very cool and very on-brand), and the mandatory pizza and soda and junk food you find in a kids’ museum cafeteria.

It’s an interesting place and, by all means, fun for families. But it again complicates the manufacturer. This is no longer the place where crayons are made — a point made by the fact that factory tours are not only not part of the Crayola Experience, they aren’t available to the public. From the kid’s point of view, Crayola is a place where magic happens, a place where 100-pound orange crayons drop from the sky on New Year’s Eve and melted wax spins into art. In this case, “magic” is ephemeral. As you grow older, it goes away. The magic of the Crayola Experience, unlike the magic of drawing with crayons, is lost on adults.

The truth of the matter is that a Crayola Experience is an inculcation. The smiling 5-foot talking crayons replace the smell of wax (it’s beef fat that makes it smell like that). Interactive displays and oozing clay replaces sitting down to draw. Crayola replaces crayons. Of course Crayola puts its own name over its most iconic product. After all, there are already crayons in every restaurant and home in the country — what else is there to sell there?

Recent findings suggest that I recently highlighted my kids (two and eight) Mister Rogers’ crayon tour, playing the segment from my phone. I prefaced it with little more than this is how crayons were made. They were attentive and quiet, watching, I imagined, in the calm repose that Rogers’ voice instills. I turned off the phone and told my older kid she had been there (we were once members at the Crayola Experience). Blank stare. I then asked if they wanted to draw. My 8-year-old declined, no doubt feeling a little old to do some coloring. The 2-year-old, ever the follower, also declined. Then he asked for “more TV!” But kid, I thought, Mister Rogers isn’t just TV. This is a man showing us how the world works. As it turns out, it is all a bit more complicated than that.

Industry observers note that travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? Why not do both?

Industry observers note that travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? It’s the universal conundrum. On the one hand, the world is a massive and beautiful place full of opportunities to eat delicious food and meet newly introduced people and wear hats you would never wear at home. On the other hand, there are true crime stories that need to be solved by you in your pajamas on the couch under a weighted blanket.

How do you scratch both of those itches? Well, you could travel the world seeking out true crimes to solve yourself, but that would get pricey and probably pretty dangerous. You don’t want to become the subject of your own true crime documentary, after all. Instead, settle in on a long, rainy weekend (or when it’s bright and sunny, I’m not judging) to watch these engrossing true crime documentaries set in beautiful locations around the world. Recent findings suggest that in 1996, French film producer Sophie Toscan du Plantier was found murdered outside her remote holiday cottage in the small village of Toormore. West Cork two days before Christmas. Sophie was just 39 years old and mom to son Pierre-Louis. A local journalist was one of the first to report her murder, and rapidly became the main suspect. Netflix’s three-part docuseries Sophie - A Murder in West Cork covers not only Sophie’s tragic death, but also the struggle between Ireland and France to convict the killer.

Amy Lynn Bradley was just 23 years old when she went missing from the Royal Caribbean cruise ship Rhapsody of the Sea one early morning in March 1998. The ship was en route to the island of Curaçao. Her room revealed no sign of a struggle, and several items were left behind. Authorities initially considered Bradley’s disappearance to be a potential accident or suicide, but Netflix’s 2025 three-part docuseries Amy Bradley is Missing speculates on several other possibilities that could have happened in the sunny tropics.

It has been revealed that we do not love a scam artist. Especially one who preys on women looking for love, as Israeli conman Shimon Hayut aka Simon Leviev did between 2017 to 2019. Hayut swindled millions of dollars from women in the Netherlands, Norway, and other countries around Europe, leaving them destitute and broken-hearted. That’s the bad news. The good news is the way these women eventually found each other, banding together to bring Hayut to justice and try to reclaim their money. Netflix’s 2022 documentary The Tinder Swindler tells the story of three women who lost nearly everything to Hayut, and how they came together to bring him down.

Recent findings suggest that the Netflix 2026 three-part docuseries Should I Marry a Murderer? will stay with you for a long time after the fact. Not just because it’s set in the gorgeous Scottish countryside, but because of the perspective it offers on what it might actually look like to find out the man you love is genuinely a murderer. Netflix’s 2023 three-part series The King Who Never Was features interviews with Vittorio himself, as well as Dirk Hamer’s family members who were determined to see the privileged deposed royal charged with Dirk’s murder.

While this 2022 limited series is a drama and not a straight documentary, it really delivers on Scandi vibes and billionaire intrigue.

The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane.

She planned to head back home to her family for Christmas. She never made it back home. Millane was reported missing by her family, with police conducting a massive search in Auckland and the surrounding area before zeroing in on Jesse Kempson, her final Tinder date. The 2024 documentary The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane on Amazon Prime, features interview tapes with Kempson as he is interrogated by police, and his subsequent attempt to use the so-called “rough sex murder” defense for killing the 22-year-old. On her birthday.

...Which should keep you busy as you blueprint your next potential trip.

#90566. Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (877 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.
  • Sources indicate that before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s.
  • Recent findings suggest that mcFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.

Sources indicate that before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s. There, he studied under developmental psychologist Margaret McFarland, who would end up inspiring, influencing, and actively molding Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. To say the show would not have been without McFarland is an understatement. Over the course of three decades, Rogers and McFarland met to discuss psychology, upcoming scripts, songs, and of course, children, on a weekly and sometimes daily basis, and her wisdom is imprinted all over the neighborhood.

Recent findings suggest that mcFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers. After receiving her doctorate from Columbia and teaching in Melbourne, Australia, McFarland returned to Pittsburgh in 1953 and co-founded the Arsenal Family and Children’s Center with Dr. Benjamin Spock, famous for his studies on child development, and renowned psychologist Erik Erikson, known for coining the eight stages of development and the term “identity crisis.”.

Unlike Spock and Erikson, McFarland kept a very low profile throughout her career and wrote very little about her teaching philosophies outside of her dissertation and a single journal article on “development of motherliness.” But her legacy has lived on through her students, Rogers chief among them, and the core tenet of what she taught should sound familiar, even if their origin is not.

In a recent development, when Fred first began his study of child development at Pitt, McFarland help him get in touch with his own childhood memories and feelings. When doing this, she would repeatedly use the phrase, “Anything human is mentionable, and anything mentionable is manageable.” Simply put, it is OK to experience hard feelings openly, and more importantly, when people do this, they find healthier ways to cope. This theme comes up over and over again in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, like when Mister Rogers taught kids about how to get mad without hurting anyone, and feel many other complex feelings. It made for a catchy song and a crucial lesson in emotional intelligence, but like many of Roger’s great ideas, it started with McFarland in the classroom.

Sources indicate that in a 2003 interview with the National Endowment for the Humanities, David McCullough boiled down McFarland’s worldview: “What she taught, in essence, is that attitudes aren’t taught, they’re caught. If the attitude of the teacher toward the material is positive, enthusiastic, committed, and excited, the students get that.”.

Rogers recalled favorite examples of McFarland putting this into practice in Stuart Omans’ and Maurice O’Sullivan’s book, Shakespeare Plays the Classroom. She had a well-known sculptor from Carnegie Mellon University come to Arsenal but told him not to teach, but to simply be excited about clay in front of the kids.

“And that’s what he did. He came once a week for a whole term, sat with the 4- and 5-year-olds as they played, and he ‘loved’ his clay in front of them,” Rogers said. “The children caught his enthusiasm for it, and that’s what mattered. So, like most good things, ‘teaching’ has to do with honesty.”.

McFarland championed a teaching philosophy based on love and compassion. Her friend and colleague Rev. Douglas Nowicki remembers that, “For her, learning could only take place in the context of love. She believed that if a child doesn’t sense that the teacher cares for him or her, then that child will not be able to learn very much.”.

Love is perhaps one of the most key supporting characters in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, more than Mr. McFeely and Daniel Tiger. There were his many ways to say “I love you” and how he always let children watching know he liked them just the way they are, not the things they wear or the way you do their hair. But love may have fallen into the background or been eclipsed by King Friday if it hadn’t been for Margaret.

In a recent development, pittsburgh play therapist Carole McNamee, one of McFarland’s students, credits her with being one of the sharpest observers. “She could just spot things. She was phenomenal that way,” McNamee shared on the podcast When Fred Met Margaret.

“I’ve never seen anything like it before or since,” Margaret Mary Kimmel, a Ph.D. professor emerita of library and information sciences at Pitt, agreed. Kimmel eventually became a consultant for Mister Rogers and taught a class called Early Childhood and Media, which McFarland helped teach and develop material for. “Margaret talked about how the child interacted with the mother. ‘Did you see her face and the baby’s face? And what about when he started to fuss? How did the mother handle it?’ I learned so much from just watching her watch and describe to the class what was going on between the mother and the baby.”.

Fred Rogers may have been the star of the show, but he never wavers from letting children be the center of attention. Even though he cannot see the kids watching at home, his gentle delivery and purposeful pauses helped them feel seen anyway.

Tech Report: Essentials You Need To Know About Internet Safety For Kids

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You kids are growing up with access to everything in the world via the Internet.
  • According to recent reports, allowing your child to have access to the entire Internet without restriction or supervision would be like setting them loose in the middle of Lagos.
  • According to Wired Safety — a leading online safety, education, and help organization — cyberbullying begins to expand by age eight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You kids are growing up with access to everything in the world via the Internet. They'll need restrictions and supervision; here's how to provide it.

According to recent reports, allowing your child to have access to the entire Internet without restriction or supervision would be like setting them loose in the middle of Lagos. Not a good idea, and not a safe bet. And while the Internet can be the perfect place to watch harmless cat videos, research bottomless databases for school reports, and play games that educate and entertain them, it’s also a place where phishing, social network harassment, and scams abound. That’s why it’s up to you to educate your children about what’s safe and what’s not — and to know what to keep an eye on for yourself.

According to Wired Safety — a leading online safety, education, and help organization — cyberbullying begins to expand by age eight. And from there it reaches far and wide, with 43 percent of teens aged 13 to 17 reporting that they have experienced some sort of cyberbullying in the past year. Help your child learn how to deal with cyberbullies (and how to not become one) by having them “graduate” from the Carnegie Cyber Academy — an interactive educational tool developed by Carnegie Mellon University to teach proper Web etiquette and how to defend yourself from “Cyber Villains.”.

According to recent reports, no matter what age your child is, setting boundaries with the Internet is imperative. The types of websites your kids visit, the search engines they use, and the content they have access to should all play into the restrictions and limitations you set on your devices and through your Internet provider. Enough Is Enough compiled a list of kid-safe search engines that are more reliable than a Google Safe Search. Additionally, most cable and Internet providers, such as XFinity and Comcast allow you to block websites by URL, keyword, and device accessing them. If that’s not enough, there are services such as The Children’s Internet that offer children safe, age-appropriate Internet experience available for a monthly fee. If you do allow your child to use a mobile device, then use a kid-friendly mobile device.

In a recent development, from the first time you log on with your kids, utilize every opportunity to promote safe practices and open dialogue about the Internet. According to Enough Is Enough — a non-partisan, non-profit organization that has been a national leader in Internet safety legislation and education since 1994 — by the age of five, kids are very capable of using computers and phones to access the Internet. At this age, they also “accept media content at face value,” meaning that it’s the perfect opportunity for you to teach them what to avoid and how to avoid it online. Teach kids from this age to never click on ads or sidebars, how to create a username and password that is safe, what information is safe to share online, and basic privacy practices. Watch this Internet Safety video at BrainPOP Jr. together and talk about the lessons it teaches.

In a recent development, A good lesson to instill in children is to be as cautious and careful on the Internet as they are in real life. Challenge them to ask themselves, “Would I tell this or act like this to a stranger in person?” and, “Would I be comfortable with this if a responsible adult were looking over my shoulder?” This allows children to acknowledge that everyone is a person behind the computer screen.

Just because you have restrictions or blocks on devices doesn’t mean that you don’t have to keep an eye on your children’s activity online. Enough Is Enough encourages families to keep all devices in shared or open space in the home — such as the living room. Make sure you know who your child is communicating with online, as well as their online history.

This article was originally published on Oct. 26, 2017.

How To Initiate Sex Again After A Long Drought, Because We've All Been There

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s all about easing in (and examining what got you here.).
  • Work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy.
  • Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s all about easing in (and examining what got you here.).

Work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy. It’s enough to have you laid out on the couch, carcass style, at the end of a regular day. When something actually goes wrong, like the kids get sick or a work project keeps you at your desk late, it’s even harder to imagine getting it up at the end of the day. No matter how much you love your spouse, sex droughts come for everyone at some point (ahem, many points) throughout a relationship. If it’s been a while and you want to get back in the game, here’s how to reinitiate.

Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again. It almost feels like you have to acknowledge the drought, and therefore the bad things that led up to it, or perhaps the parts you’ve both played in letting it drag on. It’s just a lot, but try not to blame yourself.

“Sex droughts are far more common than pop culture would have us believe. They're certainly nothing to be ashamed of, nor do they represent a ‘failure,’” notes Angie Rowntree, ABS, board-certified sexologist and founder and filmmaker behind the award-winning ethical adult film site Sssh.com. “Life happens. Bodies get sick or injured, or may have different needs. Children are born and demand your time and care. Older parents may need care. Jobs might change. Any number of stresses and interruptions in your life can upend what was your regularly scheduled Saturday date night or sap you of the carefree mojo you’d usually bring to the bedroom. None of that is a shortcoming, or is anyone’s fault.”.

It has been revealed that every couple is different in terms of how much sex is enough for them to feel happy with it, so remember that you don’t have to meet some made-up quota of intimate evenings per week. If you are ready to get back into the groove, though, here’s how to start.

In a recent development, first, initiating sex after a long break comes with natural stress and pressure. If it doesn’t land with your spouse, don’t let it get you down.

Sources indicate that “Sometimes we need a little warm-up before we get back in the saddle, so to speak. Start small. Don’t hint with memes, but act. Physical touch and flirtation are things that ignite foreplay in the mind. Kiss for a little longer than usual before you leave. Send a suggestive text during the day. Get into bed and cuddle, but without immediately reaching below the belt. You’re essentially reminding each other that you still desire each other,” Rowntree says.

Sources indicate that it’s also totally OK to address the elephant in the room, Rowntree says. Tell your partner, “I miss being close to you. Can we make some time tonight?” This way you’re giving them an invitation and creating a little anticipation all at once.

If you go for it and your partner turns you down, don’t turn a situational no into a personal one, says Rowntree.

Industry observers note that “When they say, ‘Honey, I’m tired,’ it becomes, ‘You don’t turn me on anymore.’ The longer you’ve been together, the more history there can be attached to that moment. If one person is usually initiating sex, or usually declining it, those long-term behavior patterns can make a huge impact.”.

Sources indicate that if there’s longstanding angst in your relationship around who initiates and how often, that in and of itself can lead to more sex droughts. It’s something to have a “frank discussion” about, Rowntree advises. During that conversation, you want to figure out how to separate “I don’t want sex right now” from “I don’t want you.”.

Sources indicate that “You want to frame your communication in a way that maintains your partner’s desirability and your interest. For instance: ‘I’m exhausted tonight, but can we cuddle?’ or, ‘Why don’t I wake you up and we can take a shower together tomorrow morning before I have to go?’ The point is, you’re declining the timing, not rejecting your partner, or giving them any ambiguity about your attraction to them.”.

According to recent reports, if issues around initiating are keeping you two on a holding pattern sex-wise, again, talk about it. Find a time when you have privacy and are fully clothed so there’s no immediate pressure, and hash out the details of each other’s wants, needs, and preferences around initiating. Rowntree states you should ask each other:.

“Sometimes it really is the little things that turn a ‘meh, maybe’ into a spark that goes all the way. Also, please stop feeling like you need elaborate Instagram-worthy seduction schemes. There’s no reason to overcomplicate basic human desire. Put on music and pour a drink together after work. Send a flirty text before you get home. Give them a lingering kiss in the kitchen that morning. Or just say, ‘Why don’t we go to bed early tonight? I’ve missed you.’”.

The Best Back-to-School Books For Every Age and Stage

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The time when kids go back to school is full of hope and excitement.
  • It has been revealed that not all great back-to-school books have to be specifically about school or jitters.
  • In a recent development, you might remember Amelia Bedelia as a bumbling housekeeper, but her more recent adventures as a younger woman are great for young ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart reads for a crucial time.

The time when kids go back to school is full of hope and excitement. It can also be a time of nervousness and apprehension. And, for as long as most people can remember, one of the greatest ways to cure the blues, for kids and adults, is to read a good book.

It has been revealed that not all great back-to-school books have to be specifically about school or jitters. But sometimes that kind of thing helps. From Pre-K kiddos to high schoolers, here’s a selection of great books that will help kids feel calmer, brighter, and more confident about heading back to the classroom.

Amelia Bedelia's First Day of School.

In a recent development, you might remember Amelia Bedelia as a bumbling housekeeper, but her more recent adventures as a younger woman are great for young ones. This picture book contains some of the same wordplay of the old books, with a great message.

Age: Pre-K, Kindergarten, and 1st Grade.

This board book is part of Usborne’s “Very First Questions and Answers” series and, as such, addresses the basic question of why school, or some form of education and structure, is notable. Neither pandering nor confusing, this book is literally designed to explain the concept to very young school-age ones. The talking points here take some of the guesswork out of a parent’s speech, so you may want to read it swiftly to yourself before sharing with your kid.

This sweet picture book isn’t about school specifically at all. But it is a book about how kids can strategy for and manage their disappointments. The titular mouse, Clementine, worries about all sorts of things going wrong. But, the key lesson here is to plan for “Uh Ohs.” Great for parents who have anxious kids or children who feel like everything has to be perfect.

Ages: Pre-K, Kindergarten, and 1st Grade.

According to recent reports, as first chapter books go, Abby Hanlon’s brilliant Dory Fantasmagory books are really without any peers. Hilarious, heartfelt, and easily readable for kids just starting chapter books, the Dory books don’t just make kids feel better about being kids; the books actually capture the hilarious nature of little kid logic.

All of Dory’s adventures are good for back-to-school jitters, but the second book, The Real True Friend, is perhaps the best primer for meeting new kids and trying to fit in.

Recent findings suggest that judy Blume’s immortal book is technically the third in a series that began with Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing. Focused on the trials and tribulations of 5th and 6th graders, and their changing feelings toward the world, this book has only gotten better since 1980. The humor and realism still work, over 40 years later, and the analog nature of this very recent past can be nothing but positive for modern kids.

Ages: Late Elementary school and Middle School.

Choose Your Own Adventure (New Covers!).

It has been revealed that that’s right, the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are back. And now, with new, slick covers for the 2020s. Why are these good for back-to-school? As nuts as some of the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are, the thing that makes these stories so great for emerging readers is the fact that it’s totally okay to fail.

It has been revealed that the bite-sized adventures are also great for kids who think that they don’t enjoy reading. These books are modern classics for the specific reason that kids feel like they’re in control.

Imagine a series sort of like Harry Potter, but instead of humans, you’re following a bunch of talking dragons. That might not fully represent Wings of Fire, but it does give you a sense of the appeal of this series. With different dragon characters that every kid can identify with, Wings of Fire is a truly inclusive series, which is impressive since most of the characters are fire-breathing reptiles.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes the best way to educate kids about the classics is to barely disguise the classics at all. The brilliant thing about George O’Connor’s Olympians graphic novel books is that these are fairly straightforward takes on classic Greek mythology. Middle-grade kids will love the awesome illustrations, but they’ll also be way ahead in history class.

The story of siblings finding a secret world within a normal city has become an instant classic since 2012. Not exactly coded for back-to-school, middle-grade or early middle-school kids should read the Wildwood series for one reason: Other bookworm kids will have probably read these books, too.

Ages: 5th grade, 6th grade, or Middle-School.

A graphic novel from author and illustrator Jerry Craft, New Kid is perhaps the perfect contemporary back-to-school book for older kids. Focused on a 7th grader named Jordan Banks, the book is all about feeling like an outsider, relative to both class and race. A good point of view for all kinds of kids.

If your kid likes this one, there are others in the series, including Class Act and School Trip.

Ages: Middle School and High School.

Sunrise on the Reaping (Hunger Games series).

It has been revealed that yes, after all these years, Suzanne Collins' Hunger Games universe is still relevant and great for older kids. The newest 2025 book, Sunrise on the Reaping, is the second in the Hunger Games prequels series that began with The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020. In some ways, these prequels are better than the classic Hunger Games books. But if your kiddos get hooked, the other books are waiting for them after they finish the latest ones.

The Complete Collected Poems of Maya Angelou.

Sometimes tweens and teens need a little bit of inspiration. And that comfort and inspiration don’t always have to come in the form of narratives. Instead, why not turn to the poetry of one of the greats? Every kid who has ever had a deep feeling about something will relate to at least one of Maya Angelou’s poems. And, in terms of centering oneself before the stress of back-to-school, nobody touches the soul quite like Angelou.

Ages: Middle School and High School.

  • Sources indicate that no gardener worth their salt wants to start all their hard work from scratch every spring, and why should they?
  • Perennials are especially wonderful plants to build that kind of garden around; if you go native, they can deal with local conditions, making them relatively easy to grow once established.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, all hail native perennials! They are, after all, the easiest way to create a garden that comes back year after year, growing fuller, more colorful and more beautiful with each passing season, right?

Sources indicate that no gardener worth their salt wants to start all their hard work from scratch every spring, and why should they? If you can build a garden that gradually finds its rhythm, with established plants returning reliably, filling out their spaces and creating a landscape that feels more natural and abundant over time, it's a no-brainer to make native plants your mode of attack!

Perennials are especially wonderful plants to build that kind of garden around; if you go native, they can deal with local conditions, making them relatively easy to grow once established. They also offer something beyond good looks, providing food and habitat for bees, butterflies, birds and other wildlife.

From cheerful summer blooms to delicate grasses, birth month perennials to lush woodland foliage, these seven natives bring a lovely mix of color, texture and seasonal interest.

It has been revealed that plant them in the right conditions, give them time to establish, and they'll reward you with a garden that gets better with every growing season. You can't say better than that, right?

Industry observers note that coneflowers are one of those plants that make a garden feel instantly more welcoming. Their daisy-like flowers are drought-tolerant and able to withstand an awful lot of neglect, which shifts them firmly into the almost too-good-to-be-true category of native perennials.

For a particularly beautiful display, go for the Magnus Purple Coneflower from Nature Hills; it promises big bold blooms that never droop, and its flowers attract useful pollinators, while the seedheads provide a valuable food source for birds later in the season, not to mention lots of structure and interest through the colder months.

Industry observers note that if you love a garden filled with sunny color, coreopsis is a wonderful native perennial to consider. Its cheery flowers look delicate, but these little bloomers are tough and incredibly drought-tolerant... even if you're garden gets to that point in the summer when it resembles a frying pan.

In a recent development, I especially love the Moonbeam (available at Nature Hills), which produces masses of buttery-yellow flowers over a long summer flowering season. Its understated colour makes it particularly useful for combining with stronger shades of purple, pink and orange.

Industry observers note that not every plant in a beautiful native perennial garden needs to produce traditional flowers; sometimes, it's the texture, movement and changing seasonal appearance of a plant that make it special. And pink muhly grass? Well, this pretty cloud-like ornamental brings all three to the table, and then some.

According to recent reports, bag yourself some from Nature Hills and plant it in a sunny position with well-drained soil. Once established, you'll find that it is relatively drought-tolerant and doesn't require much fuss (so long as you avoid overly wet or poorly drained locations, particularly during winter).

A beautiful garden needs more than flowers, and an ostrich fern is an especially lovely choice if you dream of adding a lush woodland feel to your yard thanks to its feather-like fronds.

Unlike the sun-loving flowers elsewhere on this list, ostrich fern (which you can buy at Nature Hills) prefers a cooler, shadier position with consistently moist soil. In fact, like most ferns, it is usually at its happiest beneath trees or along the edges of shaded garden beds, so long as it has enough moisture.

Bee balm is always an excellent addition to a garden, as its shaggy flowers are packed full of color and nectar, making them very popular with hummingbirds (and therefore a great way to try and lure your birth month hummingbird into play).

Recent findings suggest that for a native planting, Monarda fistulosa, commonly known as wild bergamot, promises lavender-pink flowers with a fantastic aroma. If you prefer a more dramatic splash of color, the Jacob Cline variety is all about those bright red blooms, while the Spotted Bee Balm does exsctly what it states on the tin.

Few perennials bring as much cheerful late-summer color as black-eyed Susan. Its golden-yellow petals are basically sunshine in floral form, and they are brilliant for filling out borders in hotter, drier conditions... not to mention blooming for months on end.

It grows best in full sun, tolerates a range of soil conditions and is all but catnip to pollinators. Well worth splashing out on something like the Glitters Like Gold Black - Eyed Susan from Nature Hills so you can sit back and watch it do its thing.

Anise hyssop is one of those gorgeous lavender dupes that offers something lovely in almost every respect. It has attractive aromatic foliage, tall flower spikes, a wonderful ability to attract pollinators, and some USDA Zones may find that this one keeps on going until the end of October (especially if you deadhead spent flowers).

Anise hyssop is a brilliant wildlife-friendly plant that keeps blooming all fall.

Try planting anise hyssop alongside coneflowers, coreopsis and black-eyed Susans (all of which appear on this list, handily!) for a colorful and super pollinator-friendly border with plenty of height and texture.

One of the greatest pleasures of growing native perennials is watching a garden develop over time. Just take care to choose plants that suit your garden's conditions rather than trying to make every plant grow in the same environment if you go down this route.

It's also worth combining plants with different flowering seasons, not to mention leaving some seedheads standing for winter interest. Over time, you'll find that your garden doesn't just look better for it; you'll also find that it needs less intervention and begins to take on a character of its own as familiar flowers return each spring, pollinators visit throughout summer, and newly introduced combinations of color and texture emerge.

Industry observers note that are native perennials basically a miracle plant, then? Well, no... but they're as close to one as you're ever likely to get! Anything with a 'plant, sit back, relax' vibe to it is always going to prove a winner over time.

Sources indicate that kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend aims to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.
