Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

It has been revealed that our house cats retain this same physiology and lack of interest in hunting down fresh water. The problem? They arenât typically chowing down on juicy rodents a dozen times a day. Which means they often donât get the moisture they need to keep those specialized kidneys healthy.

This is why 40% of cats over 10 years old and 80% of cats over 15 years old develop chronic kidney disease. After a lifetime of chronic dehydration, their kidneys simply canât keep up.

Sources indicate that nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

According to recent reports, heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

It has been revealed that lowering the risk: Genetics play a major part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which reveals up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Industry observers note that lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Sources indicate that lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

In a recent development, lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

It has been revealed that rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Industry observers note that lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a blueprint for each cat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I know, I know; poinsettias are absolutely the traditional choice for festive decorating, but there's another festive container plant that deserves a place by your front door this winter.

One of those underrated beauties that deserves its time in the spotlight, this holiday plant may not have the bold and colorful bracts of a classic poinsettia, but what it lacks in showy flowers, it more than makes up for in fragrance, evergreen foliage and year-round appeal.

In fact, if you're looking for a festive container plant that keeps on giving long after the holiday decorations have come down, it could be just the thing you're looking for (and then some!).

Sources indicate that poinsettias are practically synonymous with the holidays, and little wonder; their bright red, pink or white foliage brings an instant splash of festive color. Still, there's no getting away from the fact that their appeal is largely seasonal. They're tender plants, usually grown indoors in the US, and need warmth, bright indirect light, careful watering, and lots of TLC to keep them looking their best.

Sources indicate that once the holidays are over and those colorful bracts begin to fade, many poinsettias end up in the compost or trash. And, while it's possible to keep them growing and even encourage them to develop their colorful bracts again the following year, doing so takes a little effort.

Enter stage left, then, the beautiful sweet box (Sarcococca).

Sources indicate that obviously, sweet box offers a rather different proposition, as this handsome evergreen shrub doesn't have to be replaced when Christmas is over. In fact, its glossy leaves provide structure and greenery throughout the year, while its winter flowers bring a welcome surprise just when the garden can feel at its dullest.

It has been revealed that and it's not just about looks, either! Sweet box has a secret weapon that poinsettias simply can't compete with: its extraordinary perfume.

That's right, folks; sweet box produces masses of creamy-white flowers in winter, often tucked discreetly beneath its glossy leaves. They might not look particularly impressive from a distance, but get close and you'll discover why this shrub is so treasured, as they release a perfume often described as a combination of vanilla and jasmine.

It's surprisingly powerful for such delicate blooms, and on a still winter day, the scent can drift through the garden and greet you as you approach your front door. Especially if you opt for a variety like the Sweet & Lo™ Sweet Box from Proven Winners.

Once flowering finishes, sweet box can produce ornamental berries, which mature from red to dark purple or black depending on the species and variety. And it does all of this while standing in partial or full shade, no less!

Although some sweet box varieties can eventually become quite substantial shrubs, its slow-growing nature also makes it a useful long-term container plant. (You won't be constantly battling to keep it in shape, for starters, although a light trim after flowering can help maintain a neat outline if needed).

Just be sure to choose a pot with drainage holes and use a good moisture-retentive potting mix. Pop it somewhere sheltered in partial or full shade, and water when the compost begins to dry – just like all container-grown plants, it will need a little more attention to watering than those growing in the ground, particularly during dry spells.

In a recent development, of course, there's nothing wrong with a beautiful poinsettia, but if you'd rather invest in a plant that offers more than a few weeks of seasonal color, sweet box is well worth your time... not to mention a place in your heart. Not least of all because it's the sort of hard-working hero plant that continues to provide beauty long after the festive season has passed.

If your home and garden is full of those awkward shady spots where other plants might struggle, then, look no further! And if not? Well, still show it some love, I say – for a festive container with fragrance, character and staying power, sweet box is a very hard plant to beat.

Sources indicate that our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

What can we do to help stop this? â.

Industry observers note that I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â.

Industry observers note that what you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their crucial social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â.

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are right now targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

For many cat parents, the brand Capstar might ring a bell. This small, fast-acting tablet has long been used to kill adult fleas on cats and dogs. Now, the active ingredient in Capstar, nitenpyram, is being given an important upcoming role: treating and preventing New World screwworm.

On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA for nitenpyram tablets, allowing the common flea tablet to be used off-label for the prevention and treatment of New World screwworm infestations in cats, kittens, dogs, and puppies.

Why does this matter? Because until now, prevention was the missing piece when it came to drug options for dogs and cats. This newly introduced authorization helps fill that gap, giving veterinarians another tool in the toolbox while the larger fight against New World screwworm continues.

First things first: despite the rather dramatic name, Latest World screwworm is not a worm at all. It is a fly: Cochliomyia hominivorax. The âwormâ part of the name comes from the larvae, or maggot, of this fly. And unfortunately, this is one fly that definitely deserves our attention.

According to recent reports, the trouble starts when a female fly finds a suitable place to lay her eggs, usually in or around a wound. She can also target other vulnerable areas, including the eyes, nose, mouth, and other mucous membranes. Once those eggs hatch, the larvae get to work, and this is where the screwworm becomes particularly nasty.

These aren't the disgusting but harmless little maggots that make themselves at home in overflowing trash cans or rotting food. Screwworm larvae feed on living tissue, burrowing deep into the affected area, feeding as they grow. Before long, a wound that looks small on the outside has become a much bigger problem underneath. An infestation can cause extensive tissue damage and, without prompt treatment, can even be life-threatening.

Upcoming World screwworm has been detected in the United States, while Mexico and other countries in the region continue to deal with the parasite. USDA is maintaining surveillance and response efforts, including in Texas, where âzones of infestationâ have been established.

The concern goes well beyond individual animals. Screwworm can have a serious economic impact on livestock production because affected animals may lose weight, require treatment and extra care, or die. During a 1976 outbreak in Texas, producers spent an estimated $132.1 million dealing with the pest, equivalent to about $740 million in 2024 dollars. More recently, the disruption to live cattle exports from Mexico has been estimated to have cost that country's livestock sector around $1.8 billion.

According to recent reports, this is why so much effort is going into keeping this fly from spreading. This is about animal health, but it is also about protecting our entire food production system.

And no, the strategy is not simply âfind the bugs and squish them.â Controlling screwworm takes a much bigger effort. Authorities are using surveillance, movement controls, trapping, and other measures, along with one particularly interesting tool: releasing sterile flies.

The idea is surprisingly simple. Sterile male flies are released into affected areas, where they compete with fertile males for mates. When a sterile male mates with a female, she does not produce viable offspring. Over time, this can cripple the wild screwworm population.

Sources indicate that the good news is that this isn't something every cat owner needs to panic about. Where a cat lives, where it travels, and whether it spends time in an area where screwworm is present all make a difference. For cats traveling to or returning from affected areas, it's worth being a little more careful.

Sources indicate that with screwworm, the goal is to understand the risk before the exposure happens and, whenever possible, st ay one step ahead of the fly. When you consider that cats are experts at hiding things, including small wounds, a puncture, scratch, or other break in the skin can be easy to miss under all that fur, especially in an outdoor cat.

According to recent reports, A wound can become an invitation for a female screwworm fly to lay her eggs, and the larvae that hatch will feed on living tissue. Cats infested with screwworm larvae have wounds that aren't healing normally, visible maggots, an unusual odor, or discharge. In any situation, these signs warrant veterinary attention. If you happen to live near or have traveled to an area where the Upcoming World screwworm has been detected, be sure to mention it to your vet.

In a recent development, not necessarily. This does not mean Capstar should suddenly become part of every cat's routine parasite prevention. As a flea treatment, it is particularly effective at killing adult fleas swiftly, but doesnât provide long-term flea control.

A cat living indoors in an area where screwworm isn't present is in a very different situation from a cat traveling to an affected region or spending time outdoors there. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether your cat's particular situation calls for the medication.

In the case of screwworm, Capstar is used according to the Emergency Use Authorization, not the FDA-approved standard use. There are specific instructions for when and how it should be given.

If you're traveling with your cat to an area where screwworm has been identified, or returning from one, talk with your veterinarian before you go. International travel can also come with health certificates, inspections, and other paperwork, and the requirements vary depending on the country you're entering or passing through. Some documents must be completed within a specific window before travel, so don't leave the paperwork until the last minute.

For most cats, Newly introduced World screwworm is not something to worry about every day. But for cats living in or traveling to affected areas, knowing the risk, knowing that preventive options are available, and knowing what to look for can make a real difference. Itâs also great to know that those options include a product that has been safely used in cats for decades.

The takeaway isn't that every cat needs Capstar, but when a parasite like screwworm becomes a concern, having a preventive option available can make it easier to protect cats that are actually at risk.

And when a parasite feeds on living tissue, âbetter safe than sorryâ is a pretty good philosophy.

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

According to recent reports, halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting new people.

Industry observers note that the biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

It has been revealed that even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

Sources indicate that A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

Keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most important Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

Sources indicate that with trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

In a recent development, carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

It has been revealed that battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

Industry observers note that it can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Recent findings suggest that keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

According to recent reports, cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

In a recent development, A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

According to recent reports, it's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

According to recent reports, however, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

According to recent reports, fall-planted bulbs that flower in spring are surely the easiest, cheapest way to add color to your garden. Pop the bulbs into the ground in fall, then do absolutely nothing at all until green stems pierce the cold spring soil to light up your yard with fabulous flowers. From tulips to crocus, hyacinths to Dutch iris, there are plenty of showstopper bulbs you can still plant in November. As long as your ground isn’t frozen or waterlogged, all these beauties can be planted now, at a depth that's three times the bulb's height. If you live in a colder USDA zone and already past your first frost date, simply plant bulbs in a container in a sheltered spot instead.

When you’re planting bulbs in late fall, the secret to success is great drainage so they root rather than rot. That’s easily done by giving bulbs an inch-deep layer of grit to sit on at the base of the planting hole. You could fork out on horticultural grit, or you could simply use good ol’ poultry grit made of crushed granite like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart. You may need to protect tasty tulip bulbs from hungry squirrels, but then you can leave the rest to Mother Nature.

If it’s a while since you went bulb shopping, you’re in for a lovely surprise because plant breeders have been busy creating all sorts of wonderful new flower shapes and color combinations. From double-petalled tulips that look just like peonies to fragrant hyacinths in dramatic hues, these backyard blooms are a real springtime treat and planting them should be on everyone's list of gardening jobs in November. So let's skip straight to the good bit, shall we? Here’s my pick of dazzling spring-flowering bulbs to plant in late fall. From explaining the post-poop "zoomies" to reflecting on how decades-old feline nerve studies shed light on why cats freeze in harnesses, the hosts offer a lighthearted yet insightful look into how our pets interact with the world.

Discover the fascinating science behind feline movement, including how lower-body nerve pathways allow cats to adjust their bodies instinctively without waiting for brain signals. Dr. Karyn also breaks down why putting a coat or harness on a cat disrupts this "sixth sense," causing them to initially freeze or flop over.

Additionally, the hosts explore the difference between historical animal testing and modern, mutually beneficial clinical trials. From discussing how research into feline coronavirus treatments surprisingly overlapped with human health developments to debating why testing food or drugs on animals can be unreliable (imagine if chocolate was banned because it was tested on dogs!), this episode balances fun pet owner anecdotes with fascinating veterinary science.

In a recent development, the Mystery of "Poop Zoomies": Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how cats often sprint out of the litter box after taking a poop. They discuss how this hilarious habit stems from a mix of wild instinct (running from scent markers) and sheer physical relief.

Do Cats Always Land on Their Feet?: While cats try to land on their feet using their incredible spinal flexibility, Dr. Karyn notes it isn't an absolute ruleâpointing out that her own cat, Clutch, occasionally falls right on his butt.

How Feline Nerves Act Like a "Body Brain": Dr. Karyn discusses an old study on feline nerve pathways showing that cats can walk on a treadmill via spinal reflexes without upper brain input. This ultra-fast neural feedback gives cats rapid spatial awareness.

Why Cats Freeze in Harnesses: Because a cat's body relies heavily on sensory feedback from skin and nerves for orientation, placing clothes or a harness on them is like "blindfolding" their body, causing them to temporarily lose balance until they adapt.

Testing vs. Clinical Trials: The hosts differentiate between harmful animal testing and ethical clinical research. Modern veterinary trials often involve treating pet patients with naturally occurring conditions (like cancer or coronavirus), generating medical advancements that aid both humans and animals.

Interspecies Differences in Testing: The hosts touch on why testing human items on animals can be flawed, pointing out that many things safe for humans (like chocolate, grapes, or garlic) are toxic to pets, and vice versa.

Industry News: What Your Orchid Needs in November for Spectacular Winter Blooms – 6 Easy Tasks to Do Now

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out latest growth.
  • All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too.
  • According to recent reports, thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out latest growth. It could be a root, but it could also be the start of a flower spike – and that's why orchids in November deserve a closer look than they got all summer.

All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too. The days are shorter, and less light gets through the glass. The furnace has kicked on by now, drying out the indoor air, and the bark in the pot stays wet much longer than it did in July. Roots left sitting wet can go soft. Buds sometimes yellow and drop off before they open.

According to recent reports, thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic. Most of it is moving a pot a little closer to the window, feeling the bark before you water, or shifting the plant out of a draft. Changes made now, while spikes are just getting started, give a moth orchid a better shot at a full display later in winter or into spring.

Cooler fall temperatures are the main trigger for flower spikes in moth orchids, and shorter days may help a little, so this is the month when plenty of growers start spotting them. The trouble is, spikes and aerial orchid roots look a lot alike when they first poke out. Look closely at the tip, and you can usually tell. Roots come to a bit of a point. Back from the tip, they're wrapped in a spongy layer that goes silvery when it's dry and turns green after you water. Spikes don't have that coating at all. They're green the whole way up, and the end is rounded and closed off, kind of like a mitten.

According to recent reports, before attempting to train a upcoming orchid flower spike, give it some time to grow on its own first. When it's several inches long, push a stake into the bark close to the base. Angle it a little so you don't spear a root. Then clip the spike to it loosely, adding another clip higher up every so often as it grows. Orchid flowers don't always grow completely straight, so you may have more success with bendable stakes, like these Sproot stakes with clips on Amazon.

Industry observers note that flowers might still be a couple of months off, or longer, so Christmas blooms on every plant aren't a sure thing. Once buds show, quit turning the pot around – they'll grow toward whatever light they're getting.

Industry observers note that that shady spot that kept a moth orchid from scorching in July can be too dim by November. Low light can keep a mature plant from spiking at all, and it can also cause bud drop later on.

An east window is a good choice right now to meet your orchid's light requirements. South and west windows work too, as long as a sheer curtain softens the harshest afternoon sun – direct rays can still overheat buds and burn leaves.

Watch the glass, though. On a frosty night, a pane can get cold enough to damage a leaf resting against it, so leave some space between the plant and the window. Not every house has a sunny window open for one more pot, and a grow light can make up for that. This Sansi clip-on grow light clips right onto the pot.

Bark that dried out in no time over the summer can hang onto water much longer in a cool, dim room. Often, orchids get into trouble on a fixed watering schedule this time of year.

Recent findings suggest that so how do you know when it's time to water orchids? Look at the roots. Silvery, whitish roots are dry, and green ones still have water in them. Lift the pot to feel its weight, too, since a light one is another clue.

Clear plastic orchid pots, like these from Walmart, make it easier to check. Moisture meters are less reliable with orchids, but some growers like to use a Sustee Aquameter stick for a second opinion. It turns white once the mix dries out.

When it is time to water, give it a real soak. Take the pot to the sink and run room-temperature water through it till it pours out the bottom. Let it drain all the way. If any water is sitting where the leaves meet, tip it out.

Bark tells you more, honestly, than the calendar will. But bone-dry all winter is the wrong move. Moth orchids don't go dormant, and roots that sit dry for weeks can shrivel.

It has been revealed that kept warm around the clock, a moth orchid can go on growing leaves for months without sending up a spike. That seems a little backward, if you think about it, for a tropical plant. Cooler temperatures encourage flower spikes, and nights around 60–65°F (16–18°C) for a few weeks in fall can help. Daytime heat matters too, and a spot by a heat vent that keeps the plant much above 80°F (27°C) for long stretches can hold spiking back.

Industry observers note that cooler doesn't mean cold. Try to keep moth orchids above about 55°F (13°C), and don't park them by an outside door or a leaky window.

After buds form, forget about the temperature drop. Steady conditions matter more at that point. A cold blast every time the door opens can make buds yellow and fall before they open, and so can hot air blowing off a register.

It has been revealed that growth slows down this month, and slower growth uses less fertilizer. How much to cut back depends on the plant and where it's sitting. Under a grow light in a warm room, a moth orchid may still be making new leaves and roots. On a cool windowsill, it might barely grow at all.

Other types of orchids are a different story, and a few kinds need a drier, leaner rest through winter – check the type before you change anything.

Not feeding at all is its own kind of mistake, though, just a quieter one. Moth orchids cut off from fertilizer while spikes form or flowers open can end up with fewer blooms. A diluted dose of an all-purpose orchid fertilizer, mixed as directed on the label, keeps them going. One option is Better-Gro Orchid Plus, available at Walmart, a 20-14-13 formula sold in a 1-pound (454 g) bag.

Bloom boosters aren't the shortcut they sound like. Moth orchids fed a balanced formula will often produce more flowers than those given high-phosphorus fertilizer.

According to recent reports, bud blast is the term growers use when buds turn yellow and fall off before they open. Heating season brings plenty of the usual causes. Dry furnace air is one. So is a radiator sitting too close, or a cold draft every time the door opens. Bark that keeps swinging from soaked to bone dry doesn't help either.

Fruit on the counter is a sneaky one, oddly enough – as it ripens, it gives off ethylene gas that can make buds drop, so keep budded orchids away from the fruit bowl.

Damp pebbles in a tray under the pot raise the humidity a little, like this Brussel's humidity tray with decorative rocks. In a very dry room, a small humidifier, like this compact Pure Enrichment MistAire Studio humidifier, adds moisture without taking up much space.

While you're watering, look the plant over for orchid pests. Mealybugs usually turn up on the spike or where a leaf joins the stem. Something that looks like a bit of white cotton stuck in there is probably the long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) or citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri). Boisduval scale (Diaspis boisduvalii) looks nothing like that. You'll find it as small, flat bumps on the leaves, almost like they're part of the plant. Both pests weaken an orchid and spread to others nearby.

Wipe off the ones you can see with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. If they keep coming back, switch to an insecticidal soap or horticultural oil labeled for orchids. Safer Brand Insect Killing Soap, available at Walmart, is one option that targets mealybugs and other common houseplant pests. Test a small area first, then repeat treatment as directed on the label to catch newly hatched pests.

Industry observers note that routine orchid repotting can wait. It's easier on the plant when fresh roots are actively growing, often after flowering finishes, and root disturbance while a spike develops can set it back. The exception is bark that's broken down into mush or roots that have gone brown and soft – that plant needs fresh mix now, spike or no spike.

It has been revealed that leave healthy green spikes alone, too. One without buds yet may still flower, and there's no sense tossing away blooms you might've had. Cold glass is another one to watch on the coldest nights, so pull the leaves back if they're touching the window. Then there's the crown, where the fresh leaves come out of the center. Water that sits in there can cause crown rot. If that rot reaches the growing point, the plant has no way of making new leaves from the top again.

Most of what an orchid needs in November is a little attention. Spot the new spike, lift the pot before you water, and notice the draft by the back door. Get those right, and there's a good chance of a long run of flowers sometime between midwinter and spring. That's not bad for moving a pot a few feet.

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

Sources indicate that during our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

In a recent development, I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and claims she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

The work had become a community.

Julie claims it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â.

When someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very important companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Helping them keep those animals fed also helped them keep an notable part of their lives.

Industry observers note that I had arrived thinking I was just going to help deliver pet food. Instead, I witnessed something much bigger. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

According to recent reports, because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

It has been revealed that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

Galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Recent findings suggest that where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips….

In a recent development, it used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

For healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

In a recent development, intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

In a recent development, spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Industry observers note that alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Sources indicate that raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Recent findings suggest that winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

Industry observers note that inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

Sources indicate that if your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

Recent findings suggest that for tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Cats = happiness. Itâs an equation that neither cat lovers nor the cats themselves will find surprising, but itâs not something you expect to be evaluated, let alone proven, through scientific research. In a recent correlational study of subjective well-being across 93 countries, researchers examined the relationship between cat density, exposure to Toxoplasma gondii, socioeconomic status, and national happiness, with interesting results.

Recent findings suggest that according to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context. The key word in this study is correlational. Researchers have not discovered that happiness levels are the result of larger feline populations â ie, a causal relationship â only that there is a notable connection between countries reporting higher numbers of pet cats and those ranked highest on the World Population Reviewâs 2025 report on the Happiest Countries in the World.

So before you trade your antidepressant prescription for a kitten, there are a few things worth understanding.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood.

Industry observers note that the researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

Interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

Sources indicate that the study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

According to recent reports, we know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. They somehow have the ability to draw a smile on our face without saying a single word, simply by lying on our lap or sitting beside us after a difficult day. Emotional support comes in many forms, and cats seem to know just the right way to make us feel happier, calmer, and more at ease.

Recent findings suggest that but personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

Hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

In other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

Financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are vital too.

Sources indicate that this wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

Sources indicate that countries with more people showing signs of a recent infection tended to have lower happiness scores. To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Neither provides a perfect timeline of when the infection occurred.

Thereâs another important detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Differences in hygiene, food safety, healthcare access, and economic circumstances could influence both infection rates and well-being. After all, health and happiness are difficult to separate from the conditions we live in. Ask anyone who cannot turn on a tap and count on clean, safe water. A parasite may be part of the picture, but so are the everyday resources that help us stay healthy, feel secure, and simply have an easier and more comfortable day-to-day.

T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

Recent findings suggest that pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

According to recent reports, cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. A cat who retreats, flattens their ears, or flicks their tail may be asking for space. Ignoring those signs because a human wants affection isn't bonding; it's treating a living, breathing creature like a plush toy.

Industry observers note that good care means respecting those boundaries. Hiding places, elevated resting spots, predictable routines, interactive play, and regular veterinary care all help support feline well-being. Changes in behavior often signal pain or illness, so they deserve attention rather than an automatic label of âbad behavior.â.

And no, not every cat wants to be carried around like a furry handbag. Some barely tolerate being looked at when they're minding their own business. That's not a character flaw. It's a cat making its position very clear.

The study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

For cat families, the practical health advice is simple: litter box hygiene is paramount. Scoop the poop daily, since T. gondii oocysts generally need one to five days after being shed to become infectious. Wash your hands after handling litter, wear gloves while gardening, cook meat thoroughly, and make sure you wash and disinfect fruits and veggies before eating.

Pregnant women and those with a weak immune system should consult their doctor about appropriate precautions. During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

Ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

Industry observers note that A familiar purr, a gentle head bump, or a cat choosing your lap to nap in can brighten an ordinary afternoon and put a smile on anyoneâs face. The 3 a.m. bedroom sprints and hairballs left over the Persian rug, however, remain entirely separate research questions!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Late fall is an notable time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the initiative. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

According to recent reports, because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

It has been revealed that many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's important to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

According to recent reports, if you’ve planted upcoming perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

It has been revealed that mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

Recent findings suggest that many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

It has been revealed that reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

Your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see latest growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

While many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your fresh garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

Always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

Recent findings suggest that you can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

In a recent development, coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

It has been revealed that november is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s crucial to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

For all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

According to recent reports, winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange upcoming behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

As âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

The insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

The most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

It has been revealed that however, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

Industry observers note that on its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Industry observers note that like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

Industry observers note that some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

There are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

According to recent reports, urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral concerns, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

Sources indicate that A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

According to recent reports, keeping her indoors is especially vital during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

Responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

Until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a massive difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

According to recent reports, bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Recent findings suggest that gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

In a recent development, unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Sources indicate that bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

In a recent development, A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

In a recent development, impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.
